    Improper Integral

    Classification of Improper Integrals

    Improper integrals (also known as improper integrals) are mainly divided into two major types:

    • Infinite Integral (Integration region ): The integration interval is an infinite interval (e.g., , , or ).

    • Singular Integral (Function ): Although the integration interval is finite, the integrand approaches infinity near certain points (singular points) within the interval.

    Analogy between Integrals and Series

    Intuitive correspondence between definite/improper integrals and finite/infinite series:

    Intuitive understanding: The definite integral over a finite interval corresponds to the finite partial sum of a series ; when the upper limit tends to infinity, the improper integral essentially corresponds to the summation and convergence of an infinite series.

    The Comparison Test

    Absolute Convergence and Conditional Convergence

    Similar to the series of terms, the improper integral of an alternating function is classified into the following two cases based on the integrability of its absolute value:

    1. Absolute Convergence

      If the improper integral converges, it is called a proper integral absolutely convergent.

    2. Conditional Convergence

      If the improper integral converges, but diverges, it is called a improper integral to be conditionally convergent.

    Graphical Intuition: The positive and negative areas cancel each other out, allowing the original integral to converge; but if you fold the entire negative half-axis up to take the absolute value, the area accumulates too quickly, which can lead to divergence, constituting conditional convergence.

    Core Summary:

    The convergence of an improper integral is an extremely strict requirement, demanding that the negative and positive infinities “behave independently and converge” on their own; whereas the Cauchy principal value allows the areas at both ends to “cancel each other out” during a synchronously and equally (symmetrically) expanding process. Therefore, the two cannot be confused.
